title: RAG Fundamentals: Retrieval Meets Generation
content: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pairs a language model with an external knowledge source so it can answer questions using information it was never trained on. Instead of relying only on what the model memorized during training, a RAG system retrieves relevant text chunks from a document store at query time and inserts them into the model's prompt as context. This course walks through the three core stages of a RAG pipeline: indexing (splitting source documents into chunks and storing them so they can be searched later), retrieval (given a user's question, finding the chunks most relevant to it), and generation (handing the retrieved chunks to the model along with the original question so it can produce a grounded answer). You'll learn why chunking strategy matters -- split documents at the wrong boundaries and you separate a question from its answer before the model even sees it -- and why 'stuffing everything into a huge context window' is not the same thing as RAG: a system with no retrieval step, just a large prompt, has no way to prioritize what's actually relevant, and costs far more in tokens. By the end of this course you'll be able to explain, in plain language, what problem RAG solves, what its three stages are, and one concrete failure mode that breaks the pipeline even when the underlying model is capable.

sections.heading: What problem this solves
sections.body: A language model's knowledge is frozen at training time and lives entirely inside its weights. That creates two problems the moment you want to use it on anything real: it doesn't know about your data (your company's return policy, last week's incident postmortem, a codebase that didn't exist when the model was trained), and even on topics it does know, it can state something confidently and wrongly with no way for you to check where the claim came from. Two tempting fixes don't actually work. Fine-tuning bakes new facts into the weights, but it's slow, expensive to redo every time the underlying data changes, and it still gives you no way to point at a source for any given answer. Just pasting your whole knowledge base into the prompt ("stuff it in the context window") seems simpler, but it doesn't scale past a small handful of documents, costs real money in tokens on every single call whether or not the content is relevant to the question asked, and -- as you'll see in "Where it breaks" below -- large models get measurably worse at using information buried in the middle of a long prompt. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is the practical middle path: keep the model's weights untouched, keep your knowledge base external and updatable, and at the moment of each question, retrieve only the small number of passages actually relevant to it and hand those to the model as context. The model still does the writing; it just isn't asked to write from memory alone.

sections.heading: How the pipeline actually works
sections.body: A RAG system has three distinct stages, and conflating them is the single most common source of confusion for people new to this. Indexing happens ahead of time, offline: your source documents (PDFs, wiki pages, support tickets, whatever) get split into chunks -- typically a few hundred tokens each -- and each chunk is run through an embedding model that turns it into a vector, a list of a few hundred to a few thousand floating-point numbers that captures the chunk's meaning geometrically. Chunks with similar meaning end up as nearby vectors in that space. Those vectors get stored in an index (a vector database, or even just an in-memory array for a small corpus) alongside the original chunk text. Retrieval happens live, per query: the user's question gets embedded with that same embedding model, and the index is searched for the chunks whose vectors are closest to the question's vector -- usually via cosine similarity -- returning the top handful ("top-k", commonly 3 to 10) candidate chunks. Generation is the final step: those retrieved chunks get assembled into a prompt alongside the original question -- something like "Using only the following passages, answer the question: [chunks] [question]" -- and handed to the language model, which writes the actual answer grounded in that supplied text rather than its own memorized weights. The mental model worth keeping: indexing is a librarian shelving books by subject, retrieval is pulling the three most relevant books off the shelf for a specific question, and generation is a researcher who's told to answer using only the books handed to them, not their own general knowledge.

sections.heading: Where it breaks
sections.body: Three failure modes account for most of the times a RAG system gives a wrong or unhelpful answer, and none of them are the model "being dumb" -- they're upstream problems in retrieval that generation can't recover from. Bad chunk boundaries are the most common: if a document gets split mechanically every N tokens with no regard for meaning, you can easily sever a fact from the sentence that qualifies it -- a chunk boundary that lands between "the refund window is 30 days" and "unless the item was purchased during the holiday sale, in which case it's 60" produces a chunk that's confidently wrong on its own. The fix is chunking that respects natural boundaries (paragraphs, sections) and often overlaps chunks slightly so a fact and its immediate context aren't split apart. Embedding similarity is not the same as relevance -- a chunk can be semantically close to a question's wording while being the wrong answer to what's actually being asked (a question about "return policy for electronics" can retrieve a chunk about "return policy for clothing" because the vector space clusters them as topically similar, even though the specific answer differs). This is why real systems often add a second, more precise re-ranking step after the initial vector-similarity retrieval rather than trusting embeddings alone. Finally, even with perfect retrieval, models exhibit a documented "lost in the middle" effect: they attend much more reliably to information at the very start or very end of a long prompt than to something buried in the middle of ten retrieved chunks -- which is a direct, measured argument for retrieving fewer, more relevant chunks rather than more, weaker ones.

sections.heading: A worked example
sections.body: Say your knowledge base is a company's internal policy documents, already chunked and indexed, and a support agent asks: "Can a customer return a laptop they bought 45 days ago?" At query time, that question is embedded into a vector. The retrieval step searches the index and returns its top three closest chunks by similarity: one stating "Standard returns are accepted within 30 days of purchase with proof of purchase," a second stating "Electronics purchased through the extended-warranty program may be returned within 90 days," and a third, less relevant chunk about the company's shipping carrier policy that happened to score just high enough to make the cut. The generation step receives all three chunks plus the original question, with an instruction to answer only from what's provided. A well-grounded answer says something like: "Under the standard policy, no -- the window is 30 days. However, if this laptop was purchased through the extended-warranty program, the return window extends to 90 days, so it's worth confirming which program applies before declining the return." Notice what happened: the model didn't have to guess or rely on memorized general knowledge about return policies -- it synthesized an answer strictly from the two relevant retrieved passages, correctly ignored the irrelevant shipping-carrier chunk instead of forcing it into the answer, and even surfaced the ambiguity (which program applies) rather than picking one silently. That's the actual value RAG delivers: not just an answer, but an answer traceable to specific source passages, with irrelevant retrieved noise correctly set aside.

sections.heading: What's next
sections.body: Everything above assumed chunking and retrieval just work correctly -- the next course in this track, on chunking strategies, is where you'll dig into exactly how to split documents so a chunk boundary doesn't sever a fact from its context, which is the single highest-leverage thing you can control in a RAG system's quality. After that, the evaluation course covers how teams actually measure whether a RAG system's retrieval and generation are working, rather than eyeballing a few outputs and hoping.

quiz.question: What are the three core stages of a RAG pipeline, in order?
options: Retrieval, indexing, fine-tuning
Chunking, embedding, querying
Indexing, retrieval, generation
Training, retrieval, ranking

quiz.question: Why is 'just stuffing everything into a huge context window' not the same as RAG?
options: There's no retrieval step to filter relevance, so every call pays the full token cost
It scales better than RAG since there's no vector index to maintain or update
It costs less per call, since skipping the embedding step at query time avoids that per-call inference cost entirely
It stores the knowledge permanently in the model's weights, like fine-tuning does

quiz.question: Why does chunking strategy matter in a RAG system?
options: Chunk size mainly determines how fast the generation model responds
Larger chunks always retrieve more accurately than smaller ones, regardless of how much irrelevant text they end up including
Chunking strategy only matters when documents contain images, not text
Bad chunk boundaries can sever a fact from the context that qualifies it

title: RAG Bootcamp: From Fundamentals to Production Patterns
content: A bundled sequence covering RAG from first principles through common production pitfalls: what problem retrieval-augmented generation solves, how chunking and retrieval quality affect answer accuracy, and how teams evaluate whether a RAG system is actually working. Complete the linked courses in order.

title: RAG Practitioner Certification Assessment
content: This capstone assessment validates practical RAG knowledge across indexing, retrieval quality, and evaluation. Before attempting it, you should be comfortable explaining chunking tradeoffs, the difference between recall and precision in a retrieval step, and how to detect when a RAG system is hallucinating despite having the right document retrieved. The questions probe judgment calls, not just definitions: given a scenario where a RAG system retrieves the correct document but still gives a wrong answer, can you identify whether the fault lies in retrieval, prompt assembly, or the generation step itself? Passing this assessment is meant to signal you could debug a real RAG system in production, not just describe one in the abstract.

quiz.question: A RAG system retrieves the correct source document but still answers incorrectly. Where is the fault most likely to be?
options: Always the retriever, even though it returned the right document
Generation or prompt assembly, since retrieval already succeeded
Always the embedding model's dimensionality being too low
Always corruption or drift somewhere in the vector database's index

quiz.question: What does 'recall' measure in a retrieval step?
options: The average number of milliseconds a vector search takes
The fraction of retrieved documents that were actually relevant
The fraction of relevant documents that were actually retrieved
The percentage of tokens saved versus stuffing the full context

quiz.question: Which of these is a sign a RAG system may be hallucinating despite good retrieval?
options: The answer includes specific facts absent from every retrieved chunk
The answer quotes the retrieved chunk nearly word-for-word, with no paraphrasing or added claims beyond what was retrieved
The answer required a second retrieval iteration before generating
The answer is shorter than the combined retrieved chunks

quiz.question: What is this capstone primarily assessing?
options: Whether you can recite RAGAS metric formulas from memory, including their exact mathematical definitions and weighting
Whether you can name every vector database vendor on the market
How quickly you can answer the multiple-choice questions
Practical judgment about where failures occur across the RAG pipeline

title: Chunking Strategies: Splitting Documents Without Losing Meaning
content: How you split source documents into chunks determines whether retrieval can ever find the right answer, no matter how good your search algorithm is. This course compares fixed-size chunking (splitting every N characters or tokens, fast but blind to sentence and paragraph boundaries), recursive character splitting (trying paragraph breaks first, then sentences, then words, so chunks stay semantically coherent), and semantic chunking (using embedding similarity to find natural topic breaks). You'll learn the classic tradeoff: chunks that are too small lose surrounding context, so a retrieved sentence like 'it costs $49 per month' becomes useless without knowing what 'it' refers to; chunks that are too large dilute the embedding, mixing several topics into one vector so the chunk stops matching any single query well and wastes tokens on irrelevant text. You'll also learn why most production systems add overlap (for example a 50-100 token overlap between consecutive chunks) so that a fact sitting right at a boundary still appears intact in at least one chunk.

sections.heading: Fixed-Size Chunking: Fast, Blind, and Occasionally Cruel
sections.body: The simplest chunking strategy is also the most naive: pick a size -- say 500 characters or 256 tokens -- and cut the document every N units, regardless of what's actually at that boundary. It requires no understanding of the text, runs in linear time even over millions of documents, and is trivial to implement with a single loop over the token stream. The cost of that speed is that the splitter has no idea it's a splitter -- it will cut a sentence in half, sever a bullet point from its heading, or slice a table row away from its header row without hesitation. A chunk might end mid-clause with 'the refund policy applies only when the customer has,' and the next chunk picks up with 'not already redeemed a promotional credit.' Neither half means much alone. Fixed-size chunking is still useful for homogeneous, low-structure text like raw log files or transcripts where paragraph boundaries carry little semantic weight, but for structured documents -- manuals, contracts, wikis -- it's usually the first thing teams replace once retrieval quality becomes a priority.

sections.heading: Recursive Character Splitting: Respecting the Document's Own Structure
sections.body: Recursive character splitting fixes the blindness of fixed-size chunking by trying a prioritized list of separators before giving up and cutting arbitrarily. A typical implementation attempts to split on double newlines first (paragraph breaks), and only if a resulting piece still exceeds the target chunk size does it recurse into that piece and try the next separator down the list: single newlines, then sentence-ending punctuation like '. ' or '? ', then spaces, and only as a last resort an arbitrary character cut. This means a 280-token paragraph stays intact as one chunk even if the target size is 300 tokens, while a 900-token paragraph gets recursively broken at sentence boundaries rather than mid-word. LangChain's RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter and LlamaIndex's SentenceSplitter both work this way, and it's the default choice for the large majority of production RAG systems because it's still fast (no model inference required) but produces chunks that read as coherent units to a human, which usually also means they embed more coherently.

sections.heading: Semantic Chunking: Letting Embeddings Find the Seams
sections.body: Semantic chunking replaces character-count heuristics with a similarity signal: split the document into candidate units (often sentences), embed each one, and measure the cosine similarity between consecutive embeddings. Where similarity drops sharply -- say from 0.85 down to 0.4 -- that's treated as a topic boundary and a chunk break is inserted there, regardless of whether that lands at 150 tokens or 600. The appeal is that chunk boundaries track actual topic shifts instead of an arbitrary size threshold, so a chunk about pricing doesn't get artificially truncated partway through and glued to the start of a section about support hours. The tradeoff is cost and unpredictability: every candidate unit needs an embedding call before you've even built your index, chunk sizes become variable and harder to reason about for downstream token budgets, and the similarity-drop threshold itself is a hyperparameter that needs tuning per corpus. Most teams reach for semantic chunking only after recursive splitting has been tried and still produces poor retrieval on a specific document type, such as long-form narrative text with few structural cues.

sections.heading: The Goldilocks Problem: Too Small Loses Context, Too Large Dilutes Meaning
sections.body: Chunk size sits on a tradeoff curve with failure modes on both ends. Make chunks too small -- a single sentence, say -- and you strip away the context needed to interpret what's retrieved: a chunk containing only 'it costs $49 per month' is useless to a user or an LLM if the preceding sentence establishing what 'it' refers to (the Pro plan? an add-on? a one-time setup fee?) was split into a different chunk entirely. The fact is present in the corpus but not usable at the point of retrieval. Make chunks too large -- several pages -- and the embedding model has to compress multiple unrelated topics into one fixed-length vector, diluting it so the chunk no longer matches any single query well; a query about refund windows might retrieve a giant chunk that also covers shipping, warranties, and account setup, wasting most of the LLM's context window on irrelevant text it now has to read past. There's no universal correct chunk size -- 200-500 tokens is a common starting range -- because the right answer depends on how self-contained individual facts are in your source material.

sections.heading: Overlap: The Safety Net for Facts Sitting on a Boundary
sections.body: Even a well-tuned splitter will occasionally cut through the middle of an important fact, because chunk boundaries are set by size or structure, not by where every individual fact happens to live. Consider a document split into 300-token chunks with zero overlap, where a key fact spans the last 20 tokens of one chunk and the first 30 tokens of the next: neither chunk alone contains the complete fact, so neither one is likely to be retrieved as a strong match, and even if one is retrieved, the LLM only sees half the story. Production systems address this by adding overlap between consecutive chunks -- commonly 50 to 100 tokens, roughly 15-30% of a typical chunk -- so that the tail of one chunk is repeated at the head of the next. That redundancy means a boundary-straddling fact still appears whole in at least one chunk, at the cost of modestly larger index size and a small amount of duplicate content the retriever might return twice for the same query.

quiz.question: What is the main problem with chunks that are too small?
options: They take noticeably longer for the embedding model to process
They always cost more to store than equivalent larger chunks
They can strip away the context needed to interpret the retrieved fact
They can no longer be split further by recursive chunking, since the splitter has already reached its minimum configured size

quiz.question: Why do production RAG systems often use overlapping chunks?
options: So a fact straddling a chunk boundary still appears whole in one chunk
To reduce the total number of chunks the index has to store
To let the embedding model see the same sentence twice during training
To guarantee every chunk ends up exactly the same fixed size

quiz.question: A document is split into 300-token chunks with zero overlap, and a key fact spans the last 20 tokens of one chunk and the first 30 of the next. What is the likely outcome?
options: Retrieval will reliably return both adjacent chunks together as a pair
The vector database automatically merges boundary-straddling chunks back together once it detects the fact was split across them
Recall improves since the fact is now indexed in two separate places
Neither chunk alone may contain the complete fact, hurting retrieval quality

title: Evaluating RAG Systems: Beyond 'Does the Answer Look Right?'
content: A RAG system can fail in the retriever, the generator, or both, and eyeballing final answers rarely tells you which. This course introduces the standard split between retrieval metrics and generation metrics. Retrieval metrics like precision (what fraction of retrieved chunks are actually relevant) and recall (what fraction of relevant chunks were retrieved) tell you whether the search step is working, independent of what the model does with the results. Generation metrics like faithfulness (does the answer only state things supported by the retrieved chunks) and answer relevance (does the answer actually address the question) tell you whether the model used good context well. You'll learn why a golden dataset of representative questions with known correct answers and known relevant source chunks is essential: without it you can't separate 'the retriever found the wrong document' from 'the retriever found the right document but the model ignored it.' You'll also see why automated frameworks (like RAGAS-style faithfulness scoring using an LLM judge) are useful for catching regressions at scale, but should be spot-checked against human judgment.

sections.heading: Why Wrong Answers Don't Tell You Where the System Broke
sections.body: When a RAG system returns a bad answer, the temptation is to read the answer, decide it's wrong, and start tweaking prompts. That instinct skips the diagnostic step that actually matters: a RAG pipeline has two independent components that can each fail on their own, and a bad final answer is consistent with several different underlying causes. The retriever might return zero relevant chunks (a retrieval failure), the retriever might return exactly the right chunks and the generator might ignore them in favor of its parametric knowledge (a generation failure), or both might fail simultaneously. Consider a query where your retrieval metrics show high recall -- the golden-relevant chunks were in fact surfaced in the top-k results -- but the answer is still wrong. High recall rules out 'the retriever missed the document' as an explanation. What remains is that the generator had good context available and still produced an unsupported or off-target answer, which points squarely at prompt construction, context window ordering, or the model's tendency to fall back on its own training data instead of the supplied chunks. Splitting metrics by stage turns 'the answer is wrong' from a dead end into an actionable diagnosis.

sections.heading: Retrieval Metrics: Precision, Recall, and Their Ranked Variants
sections.body: Precision@k asks: of the k chunks you retrieved, what fraction were actually relevant? Recall@k asks: of all relevant chunks that exist in the corpus for this query, what fraction did you retrieve? These pull in opposite directions -- retrieving more chunks (raising k) tends to raise recall while diluting precision, since you're pulling in more marginal or irrelevant material alongside the good stuff. Neither metric alone captures ranking quality: a system that buries the one relevant chunk at position 8 out of 10 has the same precision@10 as one that puts it first, but the generator is far more likely to use context near the top of the prompt. That's where rank-aware metrics come in. Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) scores based on the position of the first relevant result (1/rank), rewarding systems that surface relevance early. NDCG (Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain) generalizes this to graded relevance -- some chunks are highly relevant, others tangentially so -- and discounts contributions logarithmically by position. Hit rate, simpler still, just asks whether at least one relevant chunk appeared in the top-k at all. Computing any of these requires per-query relevance judgments: a human or careful process has to label, for each candidate chunk, whether it's actually relevant to that specific question.

sections.heading: Generation Metrics: Faithfulness and Answer Relevance
sections.body: Faithfulness measures whether every claim in the generated answer is actually supported by the retrieved context -- it says nothing about whether the answer is true in some absolute sense, only whether the model stayed within its supplied evidence. The standard computational approach, popularized by frameworks like RAGAS, decomposes the answer into individual atomic claims (e.g., splitting 'the drug reduces symptoms by 40% and was approved in 2019' into two separate statements) and then runs each claim through an entailment check against the retrieved chunks, typically using an LLM as a natural-language-inference judge: does this chunk entail, contradict, or say nothing about this claim? The faithfulness score is the fraction of claims that are entailed. Answer relevance is a distinct axis measuring whether the answer addresses the actual question asked, independent of faithfulness -- an answer can be perfectly faithful to the context while completely dodging what was asked. One common technique generates several hypothetical questions the answer would be a good response to, embeds them, and compares their similarity to the original query's embedding; low similarity signals the answer wandered off-topic even if every sentence in it is well-supported.

sections.heading: Building a Golden Dataset You Can Actually Diagnose With
sections.body: None of the metrics above compute themselves -- they require ground truth, and for RAG that ground truth has two layers most teams underestimate at first. First, for every query in your evaluation set, you need the known-relevant chunk IDs from your corpus, usually produced by a subject-matter expert reading candidate passages and labeling each as relevant, partially relevant, or irrelevant to that specific question. Second, you need a reference answer (or a rubric describing what a correct answer must contain) so generation metrics have something to check the output against. Without both layers you cannot decompose failures: retrieval metrics need the relevant-chunk labels, generation metrics need the reference answer, and you need both computed on the same queries to tell whether a bad answer came from bad retrieval or bad generation. Practically, a golden set of 50-200 queries is enough to start catching regressions, stratified across query types you actually see in production -- simple factual lookups, multi-hop questions requiring synthesis across chunks, and edge cases like questions with no good answer in the corpus at all, which test whether the system correctly declines to answer rather than hallucinating.

sections.heading: Automated LLM-Judge Scoring vs Human Spot-Checks
sections.body: Running an SME through hundreds of query-answer pairs by hand doesn't scale to a CI pipeline that needs to catch regressions on every prompt change or model swap. RAGAS-style frameworks address this by substituting a capable LLM as the judge for faithfulness, answer relevance, and similar metrics, which lets you score a full regression suite in minutes instead of days and rerun it on every pull request. But LLM judges carry known biases worth budgeting for: they tend toward self-preference (favoring outputs that resemble their own generation style), verbosity bias (rating longer answers as more thorough even when they aren't), and inconsistency near ambiguous entailment calls where a claim is 'mostly but not fully' supported. The practical fix isn't to distrust automation wholesale, it's to calibrate it: periodically pull a random sample -- 10-20 examples -- of the LLM judge's scores and have a human re-score the same examples blind, then compare. Large or systematic disagreement means the judge prompt needs revision or the metric isn't measuring what you think; agreement within a tolerance means you can trust the automated score between calibration checks.

quiz.question: A RAG system gives a wrong answer. Retrieval metrics show high recall for that query. What does this suggest?
options: The retriever is broken, since high recall can't coexist with a wrong answer
Generation is the likelier culprit, since the relevant chunks were already retrieved
Precision must also be low, since recall and precision always move together
The vector database's index most likely needs a full, immediate rebuild before any further queries can be trusted

quiz.question: What does a 'faithfulness' metric measure in RAG evaluation?
options: How many of the top-k retrieved chunks were actually relevant to the question, independent of what the final answer said
Whether the answer directly addresses the question that was asked
Whether the answer only states things supported by the retrieved chunks
Whether the same answer reproduces across repeated model runs

quiz.question: Why is a golden dataset with known relevant chunks important for RAG evaluation?
options: It automatically tunes chunk size to the corpus's optimal value
It replaces the need for a reference answer in generation metrics
It lets the retriever skip embedding labeled queries at query time
It lets you separate retrieval failures from generation failures

title: Vector Databases: How Similarity Search Actually Works
content: Vector databases store embeddings (numeric representations of text meaning) and let you ask 'which stored vectors are closest to this query vector?' at scale. This course covers why exact nearest-neighbor search becomes too slow once you have millions of vectors, and how approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) algorithms like HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs) trade a small amount of accuracy for massive speed gains by building a graph structure that lets search skip most of the dataset. You'll learn why cosine similarity (or dot product on normalized vectors) is the standard distance metric for text embeddings, how embedding dimensionality (384, 768, 1536, etc.) affects both storage cost and retrieval quality, and why metadata filtering (restricting search to, say, documents from the last 30 days or a specific customer) needs to be combined carefully with vector search rather than applied as an afterthought. You'll also learn when a vector database is overkill: if your corpus is small or queries are mostly exact keyword lookups, a simpler full-text search index can outperform embeddings on both cost and accuracy.

sections.heading: Why Exact Nearest-Neighbor Search Collapses at Scale
sections.body: Brute-force k-NN computes the distance from a query vector to every stored vector -- O(n*d) per query. At 1 million vectors of 768 dimensions, that's roughly 768 million floating-point operations just to score candidates, before any sorting happens. At the 10-100 million vector scale typical of a production RAG corpus (millions of source documents chunked into a few hundred tokens each), exact search latency climbs into the hundreds of milliseconds to seconds per query, and it scales linearly -- doubling your corpus doubles your query time. ANN algorithms accept a small recall loss (often targeting 95-99% recall@10 instead of guaranteed 100%) in exchange for sublinear query time, frequently in the low single-digit milliseconds even across hundreds of millions of vectors. Production teams tune for a target recall rather than exactness, because the accuracy lost to approximation rarely changes which chunks actually end up in the LLM's context window.

sections.heading: Inside HNSW: Layered Graphs and Greedy Search That Skips Most of the Dataset
sections.body: HNSW organizes vectors into a multi-layer graph. Layer 0, the bottom, is dense: every vector is a node, connected to roughly M=16-64 of its approximate nearest neighbors. Each layer above contains an exponentially shrinking, probabilistically-chosen subset of those nodes -- similar to a skip list -- so layer 1 might hold a fraction of layer 0's nodes, layer 2 fewer still, up to a sparse top layer with only a handful of entry candidates. A search starts at a single entry point on the top layer and greedily hops to whichever neighbor is closer to the query, continuing until no neighbor improves the distance, then drops down one layer and repeats with a wider candidate list, until it bottoms out at layer 0. Because each layer roughly halves the effective search space and the graph's 'small world' property keeps any two nodes reachable in few hops, a query against 10 million vectors typically ends up comparing against only a few hundred to a few thousand candidates -- not all 10 million. That logarithmic-ish traversal is the entire mechanism behind HNSW's speed; the tradeoff is extra RAM to store the graph edges on top of the raw vectors, and non-trivial index build time.

sections.heading: Choosing a Distance Metric: Cosine, Dot Product, and Euclidean
sections.body: Text embedding models (OpenAI's text-embedding-3, Cohere embed, open models like BGE or E5) are trained so semantic similarity tracks the angle between vectors, not their magnitude. Cosine similarity measures that angle directly: (A*B)/(|A||B|), ranging from -1 to 1. If vectors are normalized to unit length at index time -- a cheap one-time step -- cosine similarity collapses to a plain dot product, which is cheaper to compute at query time since it skips the norm calculations. That's why most vector databases (pgvector, Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant) advertise 'cosine' as a metric option but actually normalize on ingestion and run dot product under the hood. Euclidean (L2) distance sees less use for text because embedding magnitude can drift with text length or model-specific artifacts unrelated to meaning, which skews raw distance; L2 stays standard for embedding spaces (some vision models) where magnitude itself is meaningful.

sections.heading: Embedding Dimensionality: The Storage-vs-Quality Tradeoff
sections.body: Dimensionality varies by model -- 384 for compact models like all-MiniLM, 768 for BERT-derived encoders, 1536 for OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small, up to 3072 for larger variants -- and it sets storage and compute cost directly. A single 1536-dim float32 vector is 6KB; 10 million such vectors is 60GB of raw vector data before graph overhead or replication. Higher dimensionality tends to capture more semantic nuance, but with diminishing returns: doubling dimensions rarely doubles recall, and past a point you're paying extra RAM, index-build time, and per-query compute for marginal quality gains. Techniques like scalar quantization (storing int8 instead of float32) and Matryoshka-trained embeddings (which stay useful when truncated to fewer dimensions) exist specifically to claw back that cost. Picking dimensionality is a real production tradeoff, not just 'use the biggest model' -- retrieval quality on typical RAG corpora often flattens out well before 1536 dimensions.

sections.heading: Metadata Filtering Done Right -- and When to Skip the Vector Database Entirely
sections.body: Metadata filtering restricts search to a subset -- customer_id = X, published within the last 30 days, doc_type = 'policy'. Bolted on naively as post-filtering (run vector search first, then discard non-matching results), it breaks silently: if the top-k nearest neighbors happen to belong to the wrong customer or are too old, filtering can return zero relevant results even though matching documents exist deeper in the ranked list. The opposite naive approach -- filter first, then brute-force the filtered subset -- throws away the ANN index's speed advantage entirely. Production systems instead push the predicate into the traversal itself (HNSW variants that skip non-matching nodes mid-search) or maintain separate sub-indexes per common filter value. Get this wrong and results look plausible while being quietly incomplete, a failure mode that's easy to miss since most queries still return something. And when the corpus is small (a few thousand documents) or queries are mostly exact lookups -- SKU numbers, ticket IDs, exact phrases -- a full-text index like BM25 or Postgres tsvector usually beats vector search on both cost and precision; embeddings win on fuzzy, semantic queries, not exact matches.

quiz.question: Why do production systems use approximate nearest neighbor search instead of exact search?
options: Exact search gets too slow at scale, so ANN trades some accuracy for speed
Exact search cannot compute cosine similarity between vectors at all, so it isn't a valid comparison in the first place
ANN always returns strictly more accurate results than exact search
Exact search requires specialized GPU hardware that ANN doesn't need

quiz.question: When might a vector database be the wrong choice for a search problem?
options: When queries involve fuzzy or semantic matching, not keywords
When the corpus grows past a few thousand documents in size
When the corpus is small or queries are exact keyword lookups
When cosine similarity isn't an available distance metric

quiz.question: What is a key risk of bolting metadata filtering onto vector search as an afterthought?
options: It forces every future query into a full brute-force scan
Post-filtering can silently drop matches that actually exist
It permanently disables cosine similarity for the whole index
It always doubles the storage cost of the underlying vector index

title: Agentic RAG: Retrieval as a Tool, Not a Fixed Pipeline Step
content: Classic RAG retrieves once, then generates once -- a fixed pipeline. Agentic RAG instead gives the model retrieval as a tool it can call repeatedly and reason about, which matters for multi-hop questions that no single retrieval pass can answer (for example, 'which of our vendors had the highest renewal cost increase compared to last year's contract?' requires finding two separate documents and comparing them). This course covers iterative retrieve-reason loops where the model decides whether it has enough evidence yet or needs to search again with a refined query, query decomposition (breaking a complex question into sub-questions that are each independently retrievable), and query rewriting (reformulating a vague user question into a more retrievable form before searching). You'll also learn about self-critique patterns, where the model checks its own draft answer against the retrieved evidence before finalizing, catching cases where it drifted from the sources. The core judgment call this course builds: recognizing when a question is genuinely multi-hop (static single-shot RAG will fail) versus when it just looks complex but is answerable from one good retrieval.

sections.heading: Why a Fixed Retrieve-Then-Generate Pipeline Breaks on Multi-Hop Questions
sections.body: Classic RAG embeds the user's question once, pulls the top-k chunks by vector similarity, stuffs them into the context window, and generates a single answer -- there is no mechanism for the model to say 'this isn't enough, let me look again.' That works fine when the answer lives in one chunk. It fails on questions like 'which of our vendors had the highest renewal cost increase compared to last year's contract?' because a single embedding of that whole question is semantically close to any document mentioning vendor renewals and costs -- a top-k=5 search will likely surface fragments of several vendors' current-year contracts (they're all lexically similar to the query) while missing prior-year contracts almost entirely, since 'last year' isn't a concept embeddings capture reliably. No single chunk contains both numbers for even one vendor, let alone the comparison across all of them. The judgment call this course builds: a question is genuinely multi-hop when answering it requires combining evidence that lives in separate documents at separate times or from separate entities -- comparisons, aggregations, or chained lookups. A question that merely sounds complex (e.g., 'what's included in Acme's support tier') but is fully answered by one well-chosen chunk is not multi-hop, and routing it through an expensive iterative loop just adds latency for no benefit.

sections.heading: The Iterative Retrieve-Reason Loop: A Worked Trace
sections.body: In agentic RAG, retrieval is exposed to the model as a callable tool inside its reasoning loop: generate a query, retrieve, inspect what came back, decide 'sufficient' or 'insufficient,' and if insufficient, issue a refined query. Trace the vendor question through three iterations. Iteration 1: the model doesn't yet know which vendors even have upcoming renewals, so it queries 'vendor renewal contracts 2026' and retrieves current-year renewal notices for Acme, Globex, and Initech -- three current costs, zero prior-year costs. Iteration 2: the model checks sufficiency, notices it can't compute an increase without a baseline, and queries 'Acme Globex Initech contract pricing 2025.' This retrieves last year's Acme and Globex contracts but misses Initech's, because that document is filed under 'Initech MSA renewal' rather than 'contract' -- a naming mismatch the query didn't anticipate. Iteration 3: the model notices the gap (two vendors have both years, one doesn't) and issues a targeted follow-up, 'Initech master service agreement 2025,' which fills it. Now every vendor has a symmetric before/after pair, the model computes deltas (say Acme +9%, Globex +22%, Initech +14%), and answers Globex. The stopping rule is coverage, not a fixed iteration count: loop while any entity the question implies lacks evidence at the same granularity as the others, and cap iterations (typically 4-6) so a persistently unfindable document produces an 'insufficient evidence' answer rather than an infinite search or a hallucinated number.

sections.heading: Query Decomposition: Splitting One Question Into Independently Retrievable Sub-Questions
sections.body: Query decomposition takes a complex question and, before retrieval starts, breaks it into sub-questions each answerable by its own single retrieval pass -- as opposed to the iterative loop, which discovers the need for a follow-up query reactively after seeing what came back. For the vendor question, a decomposition planner produces something like: (1) which vendors have a renewal in the current period, (2) what is each vendor's current renewal cost, (3) what was each vendor's cost in last year's contract, (4) compute percent increase per vendor, (5) select the maximum. Each sub-question maps to a retrieval query with a narrow, well-defined target, which tends to get better precision than one broad query trying to cover the whole comparison at once. The catch: decomposition assumes the planner already knows the shape of the data -- here, that there are exactly three vendors -- and it often doesn't until retrieval has run at least once. In practice the two patterns combine: an initial coarse decomposition ('find all vendors, then find pricing for each') gets revised mid-stream as the loop learns the actual vendor count, rather than committing to a rigid sub-question list upfront.

sections.heading: Query Rewriting: Turning a Vague User Question Into a Retrievable One
sections.body: Users don't phrase questions the way documents are written, and embedding the raw question often retrieves poorly -- query rewriting reformulates it into something closer to the target document's vocabulary before search runs. A user asking 'which vendor is being difficult right now' has nothing retrievable in it: no entity, no timeframe, no concrete subject. A rewrite might resolve it to 'vendor escalations open support tickets Q3 2026,' pulling in context (the current quarter, the domain-specific term 'escalations') the user didn't spell out. A related technique, HyDE (hypothetical document embeddings), sidesteps the mismatch differently: instead of embedding the question, the model first drafts a hypothetical answer in the style of the target documents and embeds that instead, because answer-shaped text sits closer in embedding space to real answer-shaped documents than question-shaped text does. Entity resolution matters too -- a user referencing 'the Acme deal' should be rewritten to the full entity name used in the corpus, 'Acme Corp master service agreement,' since sparse or hybrid retrieval will miss the informal alias entirely. Rewriting typically happens once, upfront, and decomposition (if needed) operates on the rewritten form rather than the user's original phrasing.

sections.heading: Self-Critique: Verifying a Draft Answer Against the Literal Retrieved Text
sections.body: Before finalizing, an agentic RAG system can have the model re-read its own draft answer against the retrieved chunks and check each claim for support, rather than trusting the generation pass to have stayed faithful to the sources. In the vendor example, the draft claims 'Globex increased 22%.' A real self-critique step re-derives that number by locating the exact spans it came from -- Globex's 2025 figure in one chunk, its 2026 figure in another -- and confirms both spans are actually attributed to Globex, not accidentally to Initech's chunk that happened to sit adjacent to it in a densely packed context window. This attribution slip is the most common failure mode when several similarly formatted contract chunks are retrieved together: the model computes a correct-looking percentage from the wrong pair of numbers. A weak self-critique prompt ('are you sure this is right?') tends to just rationalize the existing draft, since the model has no new information to reconsider. An effective one forces the model to quote the supporting span for every factual claim and treats any claim without a quotable span as a trigger to loop back into another retrieval round or to hedge the answer explicitly rather than present an unverified number as fact.

quiz.question: What distinguishes agentic RAG from classic single-shot RAG?
options: Agentic RAG generates a draft answer before any retrieval occurs
The model can call retrieval repeatedly, judging whether evidence is sufficient
Agentic RAG replaces the embedding model with keyword-only matching, dropping vector similarity from the pipeline entirely
Agentic RAG always retrieves strictly fewer chunks than classic RAG

quiz.question: Why does a multi-hop question like comparing two vendor contracts challenge classic single-shot RAG?
options: It needs evidence from multiple documents no single pass surfaces together
Multi-hop questions can't be represented as a single embedding vector at all
Classic RAG lacks any way to compare two retrieved numbers directly
The generator's context window can't hold even one retrieved chunk

quiz.question: What is 'query decomposition' in an agentic RAG system?
options: Merging several retrieved chunks into one single combined context block before the generation model ever sees them
Breaking a complex question into independently retrievable sub-questions
Rewriting the query once into the target documents' vocabulary style
Discarding the user's original query and requesting a full rephrase

title: Hybrid Search and Reranking: When Embeddings Alone Aren't Enough
content: Dense embedding search is excellent at matching meaning but surprisingly weak at exact-match lookups: a query for a specific model number, error code, or product SKU can retrieve semantically 'close' but factually wrong chunks because embeddings compress away rare tokens. Hybrid search combines dense vector search with sparse keyword search (commonly BM25, a classic term-frequency ranking algorithm) and merges the two ranked lists, so exact terms still surface even when their embedding neighbors look similar. This course also covers reranking: after an initial retrieval step returns, say, the top 50 candidate chunks cheaply, a more expensive cross-encoder model rescoring the query against each candidate individually can reorder them far more accurately than the original similarity score, because a cross-encoder actually reads the query and chunk together rather than comparing pre-computed vectors. You'll learn the practical pattern: cheap broad retrieval first, expensive precise reranking second, applied only to a small candidate set to keep latency and cost reasonable.

sections.heading: Why Dense Embeddings Miss Exact Matches
sections.body: An embedding model is trained to compress a chunk of text into a few hundred to a few thousand floating-point numbers that capture its overall semantic gist -- topic, sentiment, intent. That compression is precisely what makes it bad at exact-match lookups. A query like 'error code E-4021' or 'model number WRX-350B' gets embedded into a vector that mostly encodes 'this is a technical error/model identifier,' and the rare alphanumeric token itself contributes only a small nudge to the final vector because the model has seen it few or zero times during training. The result: a chunk discussing a completely different error code, or no code at all, can sit closer in vector space than the chunk containing the literal exact string, simply because both chunks are 'about troubleshooting.' This isn't a bug you can fix by choosing a better embedding model -- it's structural. Any model that maps variable-length text to a fixed-size dense vector must throw away some information, and rare, high-specificity tokens (SKUs, part numbers, exact error strings, legal citations, drug names) are exactly the information most likely to get smoothed over in favor of broader thematic similarity.

sections.heading: Sparse Retrieval and BM25 as the Exact-Match Counterweight
sections.body: BM25 is the workhorse sparse-retrieval algorithm and the usual second leg of a hybrid system. Unlike dense embeddings, it never compresses the document into a fixed vector -- it keeps an inverted index mapping every literal term to the documents containing it, then scores a candidate by term frequency (how often the query term appears in this document) weighted inversely by how common that term is across the whole corpus, with length normalization so long documents don't win purely by repetition. A query for 'WRX-350B' matches BM25 almost perfectly: either the string is in the document or it isn't, and if it is, it dominates the score because that token is rare corpus-wide (high inverse document frequency). Hybrid search runs both retrievers over the same query and merges the two ranked lists, commonly with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (summing 1/(k + rank) for each document across both lists, k typically around 60) rather than trying to normalize and average two incomparable raw score scales. The dense side still contributes: it surfaces paraphrases and conceptually related chunks that share no literal tokens with the query, which BM25 alone would miss entirely.

sections.heading: The Two-Stage Funnel: Cheap Retrieval, Expensive Reranking
sections.body: Production RAG systems almost never run an expensive scoring model over the entire corpus -- that doesn't scale past a few thousand documents. Instead they use a funnel. Stage one is cheap and broad: hybrid dense-plus-BM25 retrieval (or dense alone) scans the full corpus, which might be millions of chunks, using approximate nearest-neighbor search and an inverted index, both of which are sub-linear and can return, say, the top 50 candidates in single-digit milliseconds. Stage two is expensive and narrow: a cross-encoder reranker rescores only those 50 candidates against the query, one pair at a time, and the results are cut down to the top 3-5 that actually get passed into the LLM's context window. The 50-to-5 ratio isn't arbitrary -- it reflects a bet that the cheap retriever's recall at 50 is high enough that the true best answers are almost always somewhere in that set, so the expensive model's job is purely to re-sort a small, already-relevant pool rather than to search. Widen the candidate set (say to 100 or 200) if you suspect stage-one recall is the bottleneck; narrow it (say to 20) if reranking latency is the bottleneck -- this ratio is the main dial you have for trading cost against recall.

sections.heading: Cross-Encoders vs. Bi-Encoders: Why Reranking Is More Accurate and Slower
sections.body: The embedding model used in stage-one retrieval is a bi-encoder: it encodes the query and each document independently into separate vectors, ahead of time for documents, and compares them with a cheap operation like cosine similarity. That independence is exactly what makes it fast -- document vectors are precomputed once at indexing time and reused for every future query, and comparing vectors at query time is just arithmetic. A cross-encoder reranker throws that independence away on purpose: it concatenates the query and a single candidate chunk into one input sequence and runs the whole thing through a transformer together, so every token of the query can attend to every token of the chunk (and vice versa) before producing a single relevance score. This lets it catch fine-grained interactions a bi-encoder structurally cannot see -- negation, exact term overlap, whether the chunk answers the specific question asked versus just being topically adjacent. The cost is that nothing about a cross-encoder score can be precomputed: each query-candidate pair requires its own full forward pass, which is why you only ever apply it to a small shortlist (tens of candidates) rather than an entire corpus of millions.

sections.heading: Tuning Hybrid Weights and Recognizing When Reranking Won't Save You
sections.body: Hybrid search isn't a fixed 50/50 blend -- the right balance between dense and sparse signal is domain-dependent and worth tuning deliberately. A legal or medical corpus full of precise terminology, citations, and codes should lean sparse-heavy; a corpus of casual support chat transcripts, where the same idea gets phrased a dozen different ways, should lean dense-heavy. Watch for a failure mode specific to Reciprocal Rank Fusion: it only sees rank position, not score magnitude, so a BM25 list that's mostly noise (near-zero real relevance) can still shove a garbage document into the top 5 purely by being first in that list -- rank-based fusion has no way to express 'this whole sparse result set is weak, discount it.' Reranking helps quality but does not fix a broken retrieval stage: if the true relevant chunk never makes it into the top-50 candidate set in the first place, a cross-encoder never gets the chance to find it, no matter how good it is at reordering the 50 it was handed. Debugging a bad final answer should always start by checking whether the answer was even in the candidate pool before blaming the reranker.

quiz.question: Why might a query for an exact product SKU fail with pure dense embedding search?
options: Dense search only ever indexes the first sentence of each retrieved chunk
SKU and part-number tokens get stripped out by the tokenizer before embedding
BM25 and dense embeddings always produce identical top-k rankings for every query
Embeddings compress rare tokens, so near-topic chunks can outrank the exact match

quiz.question: What is the typical two-stage pattern for combining retrieval and reranking?
options: Cheap broad retrieval over the full corpus, then reranking on a small shortlist
Rerank the entire corpus first, then narrow results with cheap vector retrieval
Run retrieval and reranking simultaneously on separate halves of the corpus
Apply the cross-encoder to every document in the corpus, skipping retrieval

quiz.question: Why is a cross-encoder reranker generally more accurate than the original similarity score, but also more expensive?
options: It precomputes every candidate vector once ahead of time and simply reuses those cached vectors for speed at query time
It processes the query and candidate together, not as precomputed vectors
It runs the same bi-encoder twice and averages the two resulting scores
It uses a larger token vocabulary than the bi-encoder embedding model

title: What Is an LLM, Really?
content: A large language model is, at its core, a statistical model trained to predict the next token given the tokens before it, learned from an enormous corpus of text. This course demystifies what that means in practice: the model has no database of facts it looks up, no memory of specific training documents it can cite, and no built-in notion of 'true' versus 'false' -- it has learned patterns of what text tends to follow other text, at a scale detailed enough that those patterns encode a remarkable amount of world knowledge and reasoning-like behavior. You'll learn why this framing explains both LLM strengths (fluent, context-sensitive generation across almost any topic) and their characteristic weaknesses (confident-sounding fabrication when the learned patterns don't actually contain the answer, sensitivity to how a question is phrased, and no reliable way to know what it doesn't know). Understanding an LLM as 'next-token prediction at scale' rather than as a search engine or a reasoning engine is the single most useful mental model for predicting when it will succeed and when it will quietly fail.

sections.heading: Next-Token Prediction: The One Mechanism Underneath Everything
sections.body: An LLM is trained on one objective: given a sequence of tokens (pieces of words, typically a few characters each, drawn from a vocabulary of 50,000-100,000 entries), predict a probability distribution over what token comes next. Training runs this over a corpus of trillions of tokens -- web pages, books, code, forum posts -- adjusting billions of internal weights via gradient descent so the model's predicted distribution gets closer to what actually followed in the real text. At generation time the model runs autoregressively: it predicts one token, appends it to the input, and repeats, one token at a time, each new token conditioned on everything before it including its own prior outputs. There is no separate 'thinking' phase and no lookup step -- every single token, whether it's finishing a sentence or stating a fact, comes out of the same forward pass through the same weights. A 'temperature' setting controls how much randomness is injected when sampling from that distribution, which is why the same prompt can produce different wording on different runs.

sections.heading: Where the Knowledge Lives: Compressed Weights, Not a Database
sections.body: When an LLM answers a factual question correctly, it isn't retrieving a stored record -- there is no row in a table that says 'capital of France = Paris' and no pointer back to the Wikipedia article it read during training. What training does is adjust weights (a 7-billion or 70-billion-parameter model has that many individually tuned numbers) so that, statistically, 'Paris' becomes the highest-probability continuation after tokens resembling 'The capital of France is'. That association got reinforced because the pattern appeared, in some form, thousands of times across the training corpus. This is why an LLM can't cite the specific document a fact came from, can't tell you whether a given fact appeared once or a million times, and can't distinguish 'I have overwhelming statistical support for this' from 'I have one and pattern-matched confidently anyway' -- the weights only encode the net effect of training, not a traceable provenance chain back to any source.

sections.heading: Confident Fabrication: Why Hallucination Isn't a Bug, It's the Mechanism
sections.body: Ask an LLM about a real historical event and a fabricated one phrased with the same confident structure, and it will often answer both the same way: fluently, specifically, and with no hedge. That's because the model has no separate fact-checking module that runs before it commits to an answer -- it is always doing the same thing, predicting the most plausible next tokens given the prompt, whether or not the training data actually contained the answer. If the patterns in the prompt statistically resemble the start of a citation, the model will complete a citation-shaped string, complete with a plausible-looking author, year, and journal, even when no such paper exists. This is 'confabulation' in the clinical sense: the output is generated by the same fluent process regardless of whether it's grounded in a real, frequently-reinforced pattern or a spurious one. Instruction-tuning and RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) can nudge the model toward hedging or refusing on some known-uncertain categories of question, but that's a learned add-on layer on top of next-token prediction, not a change to the underlying mechanism -- so its coverage is uneven and easy to slip past with unfamiliar phrasing.

sections.heading: Why Rephrasing a Question Changes the Answer
sections.body: Because generation is conditioned on the exact sequence of tokens in the prompt, two questions that mean the same thing to a person can land in very different regions of the model's learned probability space if they're phrased differently -- different word choice, different tokenization, different order, extra qualifiers. A prompt worded like a homework question may pull toward the fluent, textbook-style completions that dominate the training data for that phrasing; the same underlying question worded like a casual Slack message may pull toward a shorter, hedgier, differently-sourced pattern of completions. This is why adding a single clarifying phrase, an example, or a system instruction ('answer step by step,' 'cite only what you're sure of') can measurably change output quality -- it's not the model 'understanding better,' it's the prompt tokens shifting which learned patterns dominate the next-token distribution. It also means there's no fixed, stable 'true answer' sitting inside the model waiting to be extracted correctly -- there's a distribution that phrasing steers.

sections.heading: Not a Search Engine, Not a Reasoning Engine: The Model That Actually Predicts Behavior
sections.body: Treating an LLM as a search engine implies it looks things up and can tell you when nothing was found; treating it as a reasoning engine implies a dedicated logic process checks each step for validity. Neither exists. What's underneath both the model's greatest strength and its most characteristic failure is the identical mechanism: next-token prediction learned from patterns at massive scale. Fluent, context-sensitive generation on almost any topic and confident-sounding fabrication when the topic outstrips what training reinforced are two outputs of that same process, not two different modes the model switches between. That's why 'next-token prediction at scale' outperforms the other two framings for predicting real behavior: it explains why the model is remarkably good at well-represented patterns (common code, common facts, common phrasing) and why it degrades ungracefully rather than gracefully on the long tail -- it doesn't know what it doesn't know, because 'knowing that you don't know' was never the objective it was trained on.

quiz.question: What is the most accurate description of what an LLM fundamentally does?
options: Predicts the next token, based on patterns learned from training text
Looks up the answer in an internal fact database built during training
Runs a symbolic logic engine that proves each claim before responding
Sends the query to a live search index and paraphrases the results

quiz.question: Why can an LLM produce confident-sounding but false statements?
options: It runs a dedicated verification pass that sometimes misses a fabricated claim before responding
It generates the most plausible continuation, with no fact-check against real-world truth
It deliberately fabricates citations to make its answers seem more authoritative than they are
It only produces confident errors after RLHF fine-tuning removes its original hedging behavior

quiz.question: Why is 'next-token prediction at scale' a more useful mental model than 'search engine' for predicting LLM behavior?
options: Because search engines and LLMs share the exact same underlying architecture
Because the next-token framing guarantees the model never states a falsehood
It explains fluent generation and fabrication as one identical mechanism
Because search engines rely on next-token prediction internally as well

title: Tokens, Context Windows, and Why They Matter
content: Language models don't read text character by character or word by word -- they read tokens, chunks of text produced by a tokenizer (commonly byte-pair encoding), where a token might be a whole common word, a word fragment, or even a single punctuation mark. This course explains why 'the quick brown fox' might be 4 tokens while an uncommon word like 'antidisestablishmentarianism' could be split into 6 or more, and why this matters for both cost (providers bill per token) and behavior (models can be worse at character-level tasks like counting letters, because they never see individual characters). You'll also learn what a context window is: the maximum number of tokens (input plus output combined, for most APIs) a model can process in one call, and what happens when you exceed it -- either an error, or silent truncation of the oldest content, depending on the system. You'll leave able to estimate roughly how many tokens a piece of text will consume and explain why a bigger context window isn't free: it increases both cost and, past a point, the risk that the model pays less attention to content buried in the middle.

sections.heading: How Byte-Pair Encoding Turns Text Into Tokens
sections.body: Tokenizers don't guess at meaning -- they run a fixed algorithm learned once from a huge corpus. Byte-pair encoding (BPE) starts with individual characters (or raw bytes) and repeatedly merges whatever adjacent pair shows up most often in the training data into a single new unit, thousands of times, until it has built a vocabulary -- typically 50,000 to 100,000 entries for models like GPT-4 or Claude. Common English words like 'the', 'quick', 'brown', and 'fox' each appear so often that they earned their own single token early in this merging process, which is why 'the quick brown fox' comes out to about 4 tokens. A rare, morphologically complex word like 'antidisestablishmentarianism' never appeared often enough as a whole unit to earn a single token, so the tokenizer falls back to smaller pieces it does recognize -- something like 'anti', 'dis', 'establish', 'ment', 'arian', 'ism' -- six or more fragments stitched together. The vocabulary is fixed at training time, so every input, no matter how novel, gets forced through this same lookup process.

sections.heading: Why Token Boundaries Break Character-Level Reasoning
sections.body: Because the model's entire input is a sequence of token IDs -- integers pointing into that 50,000-to-100,000-entry vocabulary -- it never actually sees the letters inside a token as separate symbols. The token for 'strawberry' is one opaque ID; the model has no built-in mechanism for decomposing it back into s-t-r-a-w-b-e-r-r-y the way you would to count the r's. It can sometimes get character-level answers right by having memorized spelling patterns during training or by reasoning step-by-step out loud, but it's working against its own representation, not with it. This is the direct explanation for the classic failure mode of LLMs botching letter-counting, spelling, or reversing a word: the task requires character-level access, but the model's native unit of perception is the token, and token boundaries rarely line up with character boundaries at all.

sections.heading: Estimating Token Counts and Why Providers Bill This Way
sections.body: A workable rule of thumb for English prose: roughly 4 characters or about three-quarters of a word per token, so a 500-word page runs about 650-700 tokens, and a 100,000-word novel is on the order of 130,000-140,000 tokens. Code, non-English languages, and text with lots of rare words or symbols tokenize less efficiently -- sometimes 1.5-2x as many tokens per character -- because BPE's vocabulary was built mostly from common web and book text. This matters commercially because every major API bills per token, with separate (and different) rates for input versus output tokens -- output is often several times more expensive than input per token. A prompt padded with unnecessary boilerplate, or a system that re-sends the entire conversation history on every turn, directly multiplies your bill, which is why token-efficient prompting is a real engineering concern, not a nicety.

sections.heading: What a Context Window Actually Limits
sections.body: The context window is the hard ceiling on how many tokens a single API call can involve, and for most chat-style APIs that ceiling covers input and output combined -- your system prompt, conversation history, retrieved documents, and the model's reply all draw from the same shared budget. A model advertised with a 128,000-token context window doesn't give you 128,000 tokens of input plus another 128,000 of output; if your prompt consumes 127,500 tokens, the model has only 500 tokens left to generate a response before hitting the limit. What happens when you try to exceed it depends on the system: some APIs reject the call outright with an explicit error, while others -- particularly chat applications managing a running conversation -- silently drop or truncate the oldest messages to make room, which can quietly erase context the user assumed was still available.

sections.heading: The Hidden Cost of a Bigger Context Window
sections.body: It's tempting to treat a larger context window as pure upside -- just stuff in more documents, more history, more examples -- but it isn't free on two fronts. First, cost scales directly with tokens used: filling a 200,000-token window on every call, even when much of it is repeated boilerplate, multiplies your per-request bill regardless of whether the model needed all that material. Second, and less obvious, is an attention effect often called 'lost in the middle': empirical studies of long-context models show retrieval accuracy is highest for information near the very start or very end of the input and measurably drops for facts buried in the middle of a long context, even though the model technically 'saw' every token. So doubling your context window can simultaneously double your bill and make the model less reliable at using content stashed in the middle of that window -- a real design tradeoff, not just a bigger free lunch.

quiz.question: Why can an LLM sometimes struggle with a task like counting the letters in a word?
options: It was never exposed to uncommon words during pretraining at all
Its tokenizer vocabulary contains only whole words, never fragments
It reads input one full sentence at a time, skipping individual tokens
It sees text as opaque token IDs, which rarely align with character boundaries

quiz.question: What typically happens when your input plus expected output would exceed a model's context window?
options: Depending on the system, it errors out or drops the oldest messages
The context window automatically doubles to accommodate the extra tokens
The model compresses the prompt into fewer tokens without losing meaning
The system always finishes the response, ignoring the stated limit entirely

quiz.question: Why isn't a bigger context window simply 'free' upside with no downside?
options: It forces every API call to consume the full token budget available
It raises cost and can reduce accuracy on facts buried mid-context
It silently disables temperature and top-p sampling controls
It shrinks the model's usable vocabulary size for that request

title: Choosing the Right Model for the Job
content: There is no single 'best' model -- only the best model for a given task, latency budget, and cost target. This course walks through a practical decision framework: start with task complexity (a simple classification or extraction task rarely needs a frontier reasoning model), then consider latency requirements (a real-time chat interface has very different tolerance than a nightly batch job), then cost at your expected volume (a 10x cost difference matters enormously at scale and barely at all for a prototype), then special requirements like reliable structured output, tool-calling ability, or a very long context window. You'll learn why teams frequently over-provision -- reaching for the largest, most expensive model by default -- and why a smaller model with a well-engineered prompt and good few-shot examples often matches a frontier model's accuracy on a narrow, well-specified task at a fraction of the cost and latency. You'll also learn to recognize the opposite mistake: under-provisioning on tasks that genuinely require strong multi-step reasoning, where a cheaper model fails silently by producing plausible-looking but wrong output.

sections.heading: Step 1: Start with Task Complexity, Not Brand Reputation
sections.body: Before touching a pricing page, characterize what the task actually demands. A binary classifier (is this support ticket a refund request?), a named-entity extraction task, or a template-filling job is bounded and narrow -- the output space is small and the reasoning required is shallow. These tasks rarely need a frontier model's multi-step reasoning or broad world knowledge; they need consistent adherence to a pattern. Contrast that with tasks requiring chained inference -- reconciling contradictory information across several documents, planning a multi-tool workflow, or debugging why two numbers in a spreadsheet don't match. Those need a model that can hold and manipulate several dependent facts at once without dropping one. The test: write out the task in one sentence and ask whether a competent junior employee with a one-page instruction sheet could do it correctly nine times out of ten. If yes, it's probably a small-model task. If it requires judgment calls across ambiguous, conflicting inputs, lean toward stronger reasoning capability.

sections.heading: Step 2: Latency Budgets Change the Model Shortlist
sections.body: The same task can have wildly different acceptable latencies depending on where it sits in your product. A synchronous chat UI where a user is watching a cursor blink needs a first-token response in well under a second and full completion in a few seconds at most -- that rules out large reasoning models with long deliberation chains, or at least forces you toward streaming and smaller variants. A background job that classifies 50,000 support tickets overnight has essentially no latency constraint at the per-item level; you can trade 2 extra seconds per call for meaningfully better accuracy since nothing is waiting on it synchronously. Voice interfaces are the tightest budget of all -- round-trip latency above roughly 300-500ms starts to feel like an awkward pause rather than natural conversation. Map your use case onto this spectrum before you compare benchmark scores, because a model that's technically more capable but doubles your response time can make a product feel broken even when every answer is correct.

sections.heading: Step 3: Cost at Volume -- Why a 10x Multiplier Matters or Doesn't
sections.body: Per-call cost differences that look trivial in a demo become the dominant line item at scale. A frontier model might run several times to over ten times the per-million-token price of a smaller sibling. At 100 calls a day during a pilot, that difference is a rounding error -- a few dollars a month either way, not worth engineering effort to optimize. At 10 million calls a month in production, the same ratio is the difference between a four-figure and a five- or six-figure monthly bill. The right move is to model cost as a function of your actual or projected volume curve, not a snapshot: prototype with whatever gets you signal fastest, but before committing to production architecture, price out the target model at 10x and 100x your current volume. If the numbers make you flinch, that's the signal to invest in prompt engineering, distillation, or a cheaper model rather than eating the frontier price forever.

sections.heading: Step 4: Special Requirements That Override the Default Choice
sections.body: Complexity, latency, and cost set the baseline shortlist, but certain requirements can force a specific model regardless of what the framework above suggests. Reliable structured output -- JSON that validates against a schema on every single call, not 95% of the time -- varies significantly across models and providers; some support constrained decoding or grammar-based sampling that guarantees schema conformance, others rely on prompting alone and will occasionally emit malformed or truncated JSON under load. Tool-calling ability matters when the model needs to chain multiple function calls with correct argument formatting across a multi-turn agentic loop -- weaker models can call the right tool but botch argument types or hallucinate parameters that don't exist. Context window matters when your task genuinely requires attending to a large amount of input at once, like summarizing a 200-page contract or reasoning over an entire codebase, rather than the more common case where a shorter window plus retrieval would do the same job for less.

sections.heading: The Two Provisioning Failure Modes: Over and Under
sections.body: Over-provisioning is the default failure mode for most teams: reaching for the largest, most expensive, most capable model regardless of task, because it's the safe-feeling choice and nobody gets blamed for picking the best. The cost is invisible until volume hits production and the bill arrives, and the latency cost is often absorbed silently by users who assume the product is just slow. The less obvious failure is under-provisioning -- picking a cheap, fast model for a task that actually requires genuine multi-step reasoning, like verifying that a proposed solution satisfies several interacting constraints. Weak models don't typically fail loudly here; they produce fluent, confident, plausible-looking output that is simply wrong, and because it reads well, it slips past review far more often than an obvious error would. Both failure modes are corrected the same way: benchmark candidate models against a held-out set of real examples from your actual task, including adversarial or edge cases, before locking in a choice based on general reputation alone.

quiz.question: Why might a smaller, cheaper model be the right choice for a narrow, well-specified task?
options: Smaller models always outscore frontier models on every published benchmark
Frontier models are technically incapable of running narrow, bounded tasks
A well-prompted smaller model can match frontier accuracy on narrow tasks
Narrow, bounded tasks actually require more parameters than broad ones

quiz.question: What is a common mistake teams make when selecting a model?
options: Testing candidate models against real held-out examples before committing
Ignoring token pricing because cost rarely matters at production scale
Prioritizing latency budgets before ever considering task complexity
Over-provisioning: defaulting to the largest, priciest model for simple tasks
