Instead of every team independently inventing its own name for 'the thing where an attacker steals a model via repeated queries,' ATLAS gives the industry a shared, case-study-backed vocabulary -- which matters operationally, not just semantically, because it lets a security team describe an incident to an outside auditor, a vendor, or a new hire without first having to explain a homegrown taxonomy from scratch.

This staged structure lets a team place a specific incident at a specific point in an attack's lifecycle -- reconnaissance, gaining access to the model, staging an attack, exfiltration -- instead of describing every incident in flat, ad hoc terms that don't compose across different attacks or communicate severity and stage to a responder unfamiliar with the specifics.

Cross-referencing ATLAS's tactic stages against OWASP's named risk categories gives a threat model two complementary views of the same system: OWASP tells you what kind of vulnerability exists, ATLAS tells you what stage of a real attack it corresponds to -- together they're closer to a complete picture than either used alone.

quiz.question: Why doesn't a standard AppSec threat model fully cover an AI feature?
options: It does cover AI features fully, since the model and its training pipeline sit entirely inside the existing API-layer attack surface
AppSec threat models are being phased out industry-wide in favor of AI-specific frameworks that ignore network and authentication boundaries
AI systems only need extra threat modeling once exposed on a public network, since internal-only models inherit full AppSec coverage
It has no built-in category for surfaces like training-data poisoning or prompt injection, and no analogue for 'off-label' repurposing

quiz.question: How do OWASP's named risk categories and MITRE ATLAS's tactic structure complement each other in a threat model?
options: OWASP covers only inference-time risks while ATLAS covers only training-time risks, so the two frameworks never overlap on the same incident
OWASP identifies the vulnerability type, like Excessive Agency, while ATLAS identifies what attack stage a technique corresponds to
ATLAS assigns numeric severity scores to each OWASP risk category, which replaces the need for any separate risk-assessment step entirely
OWASP and ATLAS were merged into a single taxonomy, so referencing them as separate frameworks is now considered outdated practice

quiz.question: Why might an attacker steering an autonomous agent's actions (Excessive Agency) be more damaging than a pure data-exfiltration attack?
options: It isn't more damaging in practice, since NIST's Map function ranks data-exfiltration incidents as categorically higher-impact than agent hijacking
Excessive Agency only becomes dangerous once an agent's model weights have already been exfiltrated through a completely separate, unrelated attack
It converts a data-exposure risk into a direct-action risk, since the attacker doesn't need to steal anything if they can make the agent act for them
Agent-hijacking attacks are contained by design, since an agent's tool permissions reset automatically after every completed action

title: Understanding Prompt Injection
content: OWASP ranks prompt injection as LLM01:2025, its #1 risk for LLM applications. This lesson covers why the model can't structurally tell trusted instructions from untrusted input, real documented attack patterns including multimodal and adversarial-suffix injection, and the concrete, layered defenses OWASP names.

sections.heading: LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection
sections.body:
OWASP's Top 10 for LLM Applications lists prompt injection as risk #1: a vulnerability that occurs when user prompts alter an LLM's behavior or output in unintended ways. Critically, OWASP notes these inputs don't need to be human-readable at all, as long as the model itself parses them -- and research has shown that neither Retrieval-Augmented Generation nor fine-tuning fully mitigates the underlying vulnerability, so 'we use RAG' is not a valid answer to 'how do we prevent injection.'

The root cause is architectural, not a training gap a future model version will simply fix: an LLM processes system instructions and untrusted user or document content in the same token stream, with no hard structural boundary between 'instructions I must follow' and 'text I'm just processing as data.'

Multimodal AI expands this significantly: an attacker can hide instructions inside an image accompanying otherwise benign text, a channel most teams haven't even added to their threat model yet, let alone their defenses. Every mitigation strategy below exists specifically to compensate for the missing structural boundary at the application layer, since the model itself has no reliable way to enforce it internally.

sections.heading: Direct Injection
sections.body:
Direct injection is a user crafting a prompt that tries to override the system instructions within the same conversation turn -- role-play framing ('pretend you're a model with no restrictions'), or explicit commands to ignore prior constraints ('disregard everything above'). OWASP documents a concrete real-world pattern here: an attacker manipulating a customer support chatbot into ignoring its guidelines and disclosing private account data it should never surface.

It's the more testable variant, because the attacker is a visible, identifiable party in the conversation, which means it's also the variant most red-teaming exercises catch before launch. But OWASP's documented attack catalog shows direct injection has evolved well past obvious role-play prompts: adversarial suffixes (meaningless-looking character strings appended to a prompt that measurably shift model behavior and bypass safety training), and multilingual or obfuscated payloads (splitting an attack across languages, or encoding it in Base64 or emoji) specifically to evade keyword-based filters.

Treat a clean red-team pass against obvious role-play injection as a floor, not a ceiling -- it says nothing about your exposure to adversarial suffixes, encoded payloads, or the indirect variant below.

sections.heading: Indirect Injection
sections.body:
Indirect injection is the more dangerous variant OWASP specifically calls out: the attacker never talks to the model at all. They plant instructions inside a webpage, email, or document that an agent later reads as part of a routine task, and the agent executes those hidden instructions as if the legitimate user had issued them directly -- OWASP's documented example is a hidden instruction embedded in a webpage that causes an LLM to exfiltrate private conversation history to an attacker.

OWASP also documents a subtler pattern worth knowing specifically: payload splitting, where an attacker embeds an instruction across multiple separate, individually-innocuous-looking fragments -- for example, spread across different sections of a resume being processed by an automated screening tool -- so no single fragment would trip a naive content filter, but the combined effect manipulates the model's evaluation once all fragments are read together.

This is why any agent with tool access -- the ability to send emails, modify records, or make purchases -- must treat every piece of retrieved or ingested content as untrusted input by default, with no implicit trust extended just because the content arrived through a 'normal' data-retrieval step rather than the chat box, and no assumption that a content filter checking any single fragment in isolation is sufficient.

sections.heading: Prompt Shielding
sections.body:
OWASP names seven concrete, complementary prevention strategies rather than one silver-bullet fix. Constrain model behavior with explicit instructions about role, capabilities, and limitations in the system prompt, enforcing strict context adherence. Define output formats precisely and validate adherence with deterministic code, not just a visual check. Implement semantic and string-checking filters, evaluating responses against what OWASP calls the RAG Triad -- checking context relevance, groundedness, and answer relevance as three separate, independently-testable properties.

Enforce privilege control by restricting the model's own API access to the minimum necessary, and require human approval specifically for high-risk operations rather than routing every action through the same approval gate. Segregate external, untrusted content with clear delimiters so the model is told, as unambiguously as the interface allows, which content is authoritative and which is just data to reason over -- and system-prompt leakage (OWASP's LLM07:2025 category) is a closely related failure worth defending against in the same pass, since a leaked system prompt hands an attacker the exact wording your other defenses are built around.

No single technique fully closes the underlying architectural gap; the realistic goal is layering several of these seven together, since each closes a different partial gap rather than the whole one.

sections.heading: Structural Validation
sections.body:
Where possible, don't let free-form text reach the model unconstrained, and don't let the model's free-form output drive an action unconstrained either. Parse untrusted input into a defined schema before the model sees it, and validate any tool-call arguments the model produces against that same schema before execution -- reject or flag anything that doesn't fit the expected shape.

OWASP's final named prevention strategy is conducting regular adversarial testing -- penetration testing and breach simulations specifically targeting injection, not just standard AppSec penetration testing that was never designed to probe this class of vulnerability. A pen test built for traditional web applications will not naturally attempt payload splitting across a resume's sections or an adversarial suffix appended to a support ticket, because those techniques don't exist in that testing tradition yet.

This mirrors OWASP's general mitigation guidance directly: treat both the model's input and its output as untrusted, exactly the way you'd treat any external data source you don't control, rather than granting either one implicit trust because an LLM produced it.

quiz.question: According to OWASP, does using RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) or fine-tuning fully mitigate prompt injection?
options: No -- OWASP notes that research shows neither RAG nor fine-tuning fully mitigates the underlying architectural vulnerability
Yes -- RAG isolates untrusted content in a separate context window that the model is architecturally unable to treat as instructions
No, because fine-tuning alone eliminates the underlying vulnerability completely, even though RAG by itself does not fully close it
Yes, but only when RAG is combined with a larger context window and stricter output filtering, per OWASP's current guidance

quiz.question: What is 'payload splitting,' as a documented indirect injection technique?
options: Splitting a single malicious prompt across multiple user accounts so each account's request history stays under the rate-limit threshold
Compressing an adversarial suffix into a shorter token sequence so it fits within the model's context window without truncation
Dividing a document into chunks for a RAG pipeline's retrieval index, which is a standard preprocessing step with no real relation to injection
Splitting an instruction across several fragments in a resume's sections, so no one fragment trips a filter though the combined text does

quiz.question: What is the OWASP 'RAG Triad,' and what does it evaluate?
options: Three separate retrieval sources a RAG pipeline is required to query in parallel before it returns any response to the user
Three testable response properties -- context relevance, groundedness, and answer relevance -- used in semantic filtering to catch injection
A three-stage encoding scheme -- delimiting, escaping, and validating -- applied to retrieved documents before they reach the model
Three severity tiers OWASP assigns to prompt-injection incidents, scaled by how much of the system prompt ended up exposed to the attacker

title: Secure Output Handling
content: OWASP's LLM05:2025 risk is Improper Output Handling -- treating model output as trusted, directly executable, or safe to render. This lesson covers sandboxing, encoding, filtering, and masking as the concrete, layered controls, grounded in OWASP's documented real attack scenarios.

sections.heading: LLM05:2025 Improper Output Handling
sections.body:
OWASP's Top 10 for LLM Applications names this risk LLM05:2025: insufficient validation, sanitization, and handling of LLM-generated outputs before they're passed downstream to other components and systems. OWASP is specific about what distinguishes this from a broader 'the model might be wrong' concern (which it categorizes separately, under Overreliance/Misinformation): this risk is about what happens mechanically once a given output reaches a downstream system, regardless of whether the content itself was factually correct.

Because LLM output can be steered through prompt input, granting an application's output implicit trust functions similarly to granting users indirect access to whatever capability that output triggers downstream. OWASP names the aggravating factors precisely: the LLM having privileges exceeding the end user's own permissions, vulnerability to indirect prompt injection, inadequate validation by third-party extensions, and missing context-aware output encoding.

The practical rule is simple to state and easy to violate under deadline pressure: if your code would never eval() raw user input without validation, it must not eval() raw model output without the exact same validation, regardless of how well-tested or reliable that specific model has seemed in practice so far.

sections.heading: Sandboxing Code
sections.body:
Generated code should never run with the same privileges as the application that requested it. Execute it in an isolated environment with no default filesystem access, no default network access, hard resource and time limits, and no ambient credentials available to inherit -- the identical posture you'd apply to any untrusted third-party code, because from a security-boundary perspective, that's precisely what it is.

OWASP documents a real scenario showing exactly what happens without this: an LLM chatbot extension lacking output validation allowed a general-purpose response to trigger administrative functions in a privileged extension, causing an unintended system shutdown -- the model wasn't 'hacked' in any conventional sense, the application simply trusted its output to route into a privileged path with no gate in between.

The fact that your own product's model generated the code doesn't change its trust level; a compromised or manipulated prompt upstream -- via the exact indirect injection techniques covered in the prompt injection lesson -- can produce destructive code just as easily as a malicious human contributor could, and often with less obvious intent visible in the code itself.

sections.heading: Input/Output Encoding
sections.body:
Model output that gets rendered into HTML, injected into a shell command, or interpolated into a SQL query needs the exact same context-aware encoding or parameterization any other untrusted string would require in that same downstream context. OWASP documents two scenarios that show how directly this maps to classic web vulnerabilities: a chat interface allowing users to craft SQL queries through the LLM, where an unvalidated malicious query deletes entire database tables; and an app generating content from user prompts without sanitization, allowing injected JavaScript payloads to execute in a victim's browser when the output is rendered -- textbook SQL injection and XSS, just reached through a model instead of a form field.

OWASP also documents an email-specific variant worth knowing: LLM-generated email templates lacking sanitization, enabling injected malicious JavaScript to execute in vulnerable email clients that render HTML content -- a context many teams don't initially think to threat-model at all, since 'email' doesn't intuitively read as a code-execution surface the way a web page does.

The output being 'from the AI' doesn't change what sink it's landing in -- a string headed for a SQL query needs parameterized queries, a string headed for a DOM needs HTML-escaping, and a string headed for a shell needs argument-array execution rather than string concatenation, regardless of which system produced the string in the first place.

sections.heading: Content Filtering
sections.body:
Filter generated content against your policy before it reaches a user -- for toxicity and policy-violating instructions, obviously, but also for content that could function as a secondary injection payload if it's later re-consumed by another system, another agent, or the same agent in a future turn.

OWASP documents a scenario that shows exactly this compounding risk: LLM code generation can hallucinate non-existent package names with enough plausibility that a developer downloads and installs a malicious package published under that hallucinated name -- a single ungrounded claim from the model becoming an actual supply-chain compromise once a human trusts it and acts on it. A response that's merely embarrassing if a human reads it can become a genuine security incident if it's fed back into an automated pipeline that trusts its own prior output implicitly, which is an increasingly common pattern in multi-step agent workflows.

OWASP's Content Security Policy recommendation applies here directly: a strict CSP substantially reduces the blast radius of any XSS payload that slips past earlier filtering layers, functioning as a last line of defense rather than the primary control.

sections.heading: Data Masking
sections.body:
Avoid round-tripping sensitive data through a model unmasked whenever the model doesn't strictly need the real values to do its job. If PII or credentials pass through a prompt purely for context, mask or tokenize them beforehand and only re-insert the real values in a trusted layer after the model responds -- a token like CUSTOMER_NAME_1 carries the same contextual signal the model needs without the underlying real value ever entering the completion.

OWASP's Sensitive Information Disclosure guidance names the same technique from the privacy side, alongside two additional options worth having in the toolkit for higher-sensitivity cases: homomorphic encryption (letting computation happen on encrypted data without ever decrypting it) and federated learning (training across decentralized data sources so raw sensitive data never needs to be centralized for a model to learn from it at all).

This way, a leaked, logged, or misrouted completion doesn't leak the underlying sensitive data along with it, even in a worst-case failure elsewhere in the pipeline -- the masking layer is what keeps a pipeline failure from automatically becoming a data breach.

quiz.question: How does OWASP distinguish LLM05:2025 Improper Output Handling from the separate Misinformation risk category?
options: Improper Output Handling covers only text-based outputs, while Misinformation covers only code and other structured-data outputs specifically
Misinformation is the mechanical-handling risk, while Improper Output Handling covers whether the model's claims are factually accurate
Improper Output Handling concerns what happens once output reaches a downstream system, while Misinformation concerns whether the content is true
The two categories are distinguished by which OWASP revision introduced them, with no real difference in what each one covers

quiz.question: In OWASP's documented email-template scenario, why is 'email' a code-execution surface many teams don't initially threat-model?
options: LLM-generated email templates without sanitization can let injected JavaScript execute in HTML-rendering clients, a risk teams rarely expect
Because email templates are compiled server-side into executable binaries before delivery, a step standard web pages never go through
Because email clients automatically execute any script tag present in an attachment, regardless of how the surrounding message body gets rendered
Because SMTP relays cache and re-execute prior message content, letting an old injected payload resurface in a later, unrelated email

quiz.question: Besides tokenizing/masking PII, what two additional privacy-preserving techniques does OWASP name for higher-sensitivity cases?
options: Differential privacy and k-anonymity, both applied by injecting statistical noise directly into the model's prompt template
Data minimization and consent banners, both handled entirely at the user-interface layer rather than within the model pipeline
Model distillation and quantization, both of which reduce a model's memorized training data as a side effect of shrinking it
Homomorphic encryption, computing on encrypted data without decrypting it, and federated learning across decentralized data sources

title: Securing the AI Supply Chain
content: OWASP's LLM03:2025 Supply Chain risk, backed by real named incidents -- PoisonGPT, a fake backdoored WizardLM release, and a GPU memory-leak CVE -- shows the AI supply chain extends far beyond classic code dependencies. This lesson covers what to actually check before adopting a third-party model.

sections.heading: LLM03:2025 Supply Chain Vulnerabilities
sections.body:
OWASP's Top 10 for LLM Applications names this LLM03:2025: LLM supply chains face vulnerabilities affecting training data, models, and deployment integrity, extending well past traditional third-party package risk to include tampered pre-trained models and poisoned datasets -- and modern fine-tuning techniques like LoRA and PEFT, especially on collaborative platforms like Hugging Face, introduce entirely new risk surfaces that didn't exist in a pre-LLM supply chain.

OWASP's documented case studies make this concrete rather than hypothetical. PoisonGPT demonstrated bypassing Hugging Face's own safety scanning by directly editing model parameters to spread targeted misinformation, with the tampering invisible to standard benchmark evaluation. A fake version of WizardLM, published after the legitimate model's removal, contained embedded malware and backdoors distributed under the trusted original name. CVE-2023-4969 (nicknamed 'LeftoverLocals') showed attackers recovering sensitive data by exploiting leaked GPU memory left behind from a previous inference job on shared infrastructure.

Unlike a source-code dependency, none of these three required a visible code change a reviewer could have caught -- the compromise lived in weights, in a trusted-looking filename, or in hardware-level memory handling, three places traditional code review was never built to look.

sections.heading: Model Provenance
sections.body:
Before adopting a pretrained model, verify where it actually came from: who trained it, on what data, and whether the published weights actually match what the accompanying model card claims. OWASP documents that model-merge services -- convenient tools for combining or converting model formats -- have themselves been exploited to inject malware into otherwise-legitimate public models, and that 116 Google Play apps were found shipping tampered on-device models that silently redirected users to scam sites once swapped in for the legitimate version.

Model repositories can host tampered checkpoints under a legitimate-looking name and a plausible-sounding description -- exactly the WizardLM pattern -- and unlike a source-code dependency, you generally can't 'read the diff' on a set of weights to spot the tampering directly. OWASP's concrete mitigation: use third-party integrity checks, code signing, and file hashes to verify a model matches its claimed provenance before it ever enters your pipeline, not just once at initial adoption but on every subsequent version pull.

Provenance has to be established through the publisher's reputation, cryptographic verification where available, and independent behavioral testing against known benchmarks -- not through inspection of the artifact itself, since PoisonGPT proved that benchmark performance alone doesn't detect targeted tampering.

sections.heading: Dependency Scanning
sections.body:
Extend your existing software composition analysis tooling to cover ML-specific formats, not just traditional package manifests. Pickled model files in particular are a well-known code-execution vector, since Python's unpickling process can run arbitrary code by design as part of deserialization -- a malicious pickle file doesn't need any additional vulnerability to compromise a host, the format itself is the vulnerability.

OWASP's mitigation guidance for the related Data and Model Poisoning risk names a specific complementary tool worth adopting alongside format scanning: data version control (DVC), which lets a team detect unexpected dataset manipulation between training runs, the same way source control detects unexpected code changes between commits -- catching a poisoning attempt at the data layer even if it slips past model-level scanning entirely.

Scan explicitly for unsafe serialization formats and prefer safer alternatives (like safetensors) the same deliberate way you'd scan for known-vulnerable package versions in a traditional dependency audit, and treat a 'we don't scan model files because they're not code' policy as the exact gap PoisonGPT and the WizardLM incident both exploited.

sections.heading: Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) for AI
sections.body:
An AI-aware SBOM extends the traditional code SBOM with model-specific fields: the training data sources behind a given checkpoint, its fine-tuning lineage, and every upstream base model it was derived from, several layers deep if necessary. OWASP names a specific existing standard worth adopting rather than inventing one from scratch: CycloneDX, which already supports tracking AI/ML components alongside traditional software dependencies in a single machine-readable format.

Without this, when a vulnerability, a licensing issue, or a documented bias problem surfaces in a widely-used base model months after you adopted it, there's no fast way to answer 'which of our shipped products actually depend on this' -- the question that determines your actual incident-response scope, versus one you're left answering by manually re-tracing every model adoption decision your team has made, the same slow reconstruction the LeftoverLocals and WizardLM incidents both would have demanded without one.

OWASP also flags licensing risk as its own line item within supply chain: diverse software and dataset licenses across a multi-model pipeline create real legal compliance exposure that a code-only SBOM would never surface at all.

sections.heading: Third-Party Risk Management
sections.body:
This connects directly to OWASP's LLM10:2025 risk, Unbounded Consumption, which reframes what used to be called 'model theft' as part of a broader resource-abuse category: unrestricted querying against your model can be used both to extract its behavior for a competing product and to simply exhaust compute resources at your expense, and every third party you grant API access, fine-tuning access, or weight access to expands that exposure by one more party that could leak, be breached, or misuse it.

OWASP's supply-chain mitigation guidance is specific about the vetting process rather than leaving it vague: review a supplier's terms and conditions and privacy policy on a recurring basis, not just once at signing, since OWASP documents a real pattern where a vendor's T&Cs quietly changed after adoption to permit training on previously-protected customer data. Conduct AI red-teaming against third-party models using established benchmarks like Decoding Trust before adoption, the same way you'd pen-test any other vendor integration before it touches production traffic.

A model's weights are IP in exactly the same sense your source code is, and should be governed by the same vendor-risk process, not a lighter one just because the artifact is unfamiliar to whoever runs your existing vendor-security review.

quiz.question: What did the PoisonGPT case study demonstrate about supply-chain compromise in AI models?
options: That Hugging Face's safety scanning catches all parameter-level tampering, making PoisonGPT a proof-of-concept that failed in practice
That an attacker bypassed Hugging Face's scanning by editing model parameters directly, spreading misinformation invisible to benchmarks
That model tampering is always detectable through standard benchmark evaluation, even when the underlying weights have been edited directly
That poisoning can only be introduced during the original training run, not through post-hoc edits to an already-published model

quiz.question: Why can't 'reading the diff' on a set of model weights catch the kind of tampering seen in the WizardLM incident?
options: It can -- model repositories generate a human-readable weight diff automatically, the same way source-control platforms generate a code diff
Because the WizardLM incident involved a compromised training script, not the published weights themselves, so a weight diff was never the relevant check
A tampered model can be published under a legitimate-looking name, and weights don't have a human-readable diff a reviewer can meaningfully inspect for changes
Because reviewing a weight diff would require retraining the entire model from scratch first, making it impractical rather than technically impossible

quiz.question: How does OWASP's LLM10:2025 Unbounded Consumption reframe what used to be called 'Model Theft'?
options: It broadens model theft into a resource-abuse category covering both behavior extraction via unrestricted querying and simple compute exhaustion
It narrows the definition to cover only cases where an attacker gains direct access to the physical server hosting the model weights
It reclassifies model theft as a training-time-only risk, severing any connection to inference-time querying behavior against a deployed endpoint
It replaces model theft entirely with a purely legal and intellectual-property framing, dropping the technical resource-exhaustion angle

title: Adversarial Tactics with MITRE ATLAS
content: MITRE ATLAS gives security teams a shared, case-study-backed vocabulary for adversary behavior against AI systems, mirroring MITRE ATT&CK's structure for traditional IT. This lesson covers how to use it alongside NIST's named security-evaluation practices to map attack surface, prioritize defenses, and run incident response for AI-specific failures.

sections.heading: What Is MITRE ATLAS
sections.body:
MITRE ATLAS (Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems) is a knowledge base of real, observed adversary tactics and techniques targeting AI systems, structured after its sibling framework MITRE ATT&CK. Instead of every team independently inventing its own name for 'the thing where an attacker steals a model via repeated queries,' ATLAS gives the industry a shared, case-study-backed vocabulary -- which matters operationally, not just semantically, because it lets a security team describe an incident to an outside auditor, a vendor, or a new hire without first having to explain a homegrown taxonomy from scratch.

NIST's AI Risk Management Framework converges on the same need for shared vocabulary from a measurement angle rather than a taxonomy angle: its Measure function explicitly calls for establishing and tracking 'AI system security tests and metrics (e.g., red-teaming activities, frequency and rate of anomalous events, system down-time, incident response times, time-to-bypass, etc.)' -- concrete, comparable numbers that only mean something once a team has already agreed, via something like ATLAS, on what category of attack each metric is actually measuring.

The two frameworks solve adjacent problems: ATLAS answers 'what happened and at what stage,' NIST's Measure function answers 'how do we quantify whether our defenses against it are actually working.'

sections.heading: Tactic Matrix
sections.body:
Like ATT&CK, ATLAS organizes techniques under tactic stages representing an attacker's goal at each point in an operation: reconnaissance and resource development, gaining initial access, interacting directly with the ML model itself, executing an attack, and eventually exfiltration or impact. This staged structure lets a team place a specific incident at a specific point in an attack's lifecycle -- 'this was a model-access-stage query pattern, not yet exfiltration' -- instead of describing every incident in flat, ad hoc terms.

Cross-referencing this against OWASP's named risk categories from earlier in this track sharpens the picture further: a prompt injection (OWASP LLM01) is typically an initial-access or execution-stage technique in ATLAS terms, while a model-extraction attempt via unrestricted querying (OWASP LLM10, Unbounded Consumption) sits at the model-access and exfiltration stages. Neither framework alone tells you both what kind of vulnerability you're facing and where in an attack's progression a specific observed behavior sits -- using them together does.

NIST's Measure function reinforces watermarking specifically as a named countermeasure against the model-access-stage extraction attempts ATLAS catalogs, giving teams a concrete technical control to pair with the tactic-level awareness ATLAS provides.

sections.heading: Defense Mapping
sections.body:
The practical value of a tactics framework is mapping each stage directly to a concrete, implementable control, not just a category label. Restrict and rate-limit access to inference endpoints to blunt model-extraction attempts at the model-access stage, and pair that restriction with the watermarking techniques NIST's Measure function names explicitly as a countermeasure against data and model extraction attacks.

Validate and provenance-check training data to blunt poisoning at the resource-development stage, using the data version control practices covered in the supply-chain lesson. Apply least-privilege access plus mandatory human-in-the-loop review to blunt an agent being hijacked into taking destructive actions at the execution stage -- directly mitigating OWASP's Excessive Agency risk at exactly the ATLAS-defined stage where it manifests.

Each ATLAS tactic should map to a named owner and a specific control in your system's actual defenses, not remain a purely descriptive label used only after an incident already happened -- a mapping exercise NIST's Measure function backs with a concrete deliverable: 'establish and track AI system security tests and metrics' per control, so each mapped defense has a number attached proving it's actually being exercised, not just documented once and forgotten.

sections.heading: Incident Response for AI
sections.body:
Standard incident-response playbooks assume you can patch the vulnerable code and redeploy, which resolves most traditional software incidents. AI incidents often require additional steps a typical IR runbook doesn't cover: rolling back to a known-good model checkpoint rather than a known-good code commit, tracing which specific training data or pipeline run a poisoning attack actually touched, and re-evaluating whether other models trained on that same upstream pipeline are also compromised.

NIST's Manage function names the specific downstream discipline that makes this last step tractable rather than a scramble: maintain both an error/incident database (date, count, impact assessment, response) and a separate system change database (reasons, testing, deployment details, version history) as standing artifacts, not something assembled for the first time during the incident itself. Without the AI-aware SBOM and DVC lineage tracking covered in the supply-chain lesson, most teams discover during their first real AI incident that they can't actually answer 'what else does this affect' quickly, because the lineage tracking was never built before it was needed.

NIST's Manage function also calls for sharing error, near-miss, and attack-pattern information with external incident databases -- treating a single team's incident as data other organizations should be able to learn from, the same collaborative instinct that built the AI Incident Database and MITRE ATLAS's case-study catalog in the first place.

sections.heading: Continuous Monitoring
sections.body:
This is where ATLAS connects directly back to NIST's AI Risk Management Framework: identifying risk once at design time isn't sufficient, because new adversarial techniques against AI systems get documented and published constantly, often faster than internal review cycles can absorb them. NIST's Manage function frames ongoing monitoring and mitigation as continuing after deployment, not a one-time pre-launch checklist -- naming specific recurring practices like red-teaming exercises 'at prescribed intervals' and tracking dataset modifications over time, not just at initial launch.

In practice this means a recurring, scheduled review of new ATLAS-cataloged techniques against your own deployed systems, cross-checked against the specific security metrics NIST's Measure function calls for tracking (time-to-bypass, incident response times, rate of anomalous events) -- not a threat model that gets revisited only when something has already gone wrong.

The teams that get caught flat-footed by a new attack technique are rarely the ones whose original threat model was incomplete -- they're the ones whose threat model was never revisited after the day it was first written, while the ATLAS catalog and OWASP's own risk list kept moving underneath them.

quiz.question: How do MITRE ATLAS and NIST's AI RMF Measure function address complementary parts of the same problem?
options: ATLAS defines the metrics teams should track, while NIST's Measure function supplies the shared vocabulary for naming each attack stage
ATLAS applies only to post-incident forensics work, while NIST's Measure function applies only to pre-launch risk assessment planning
The two overlap entirely, since NIST's Measure function was reportedly built directly on top of the ATLAS tactic matrix as its sole data source
ATLAS provides a shared vocabulary for what happened and at what stage, while NIST's Measure function supplies metrics like time-to-bypass

quiz.question: Why do AI incidents often require rolling back to a known-good model checkpoint and tracing training-data lineage, beyond a standard patch-and-redeploy playbook?
options: Because AI incidents always originate in the inference API layer, so checkpoint rollback is precautionary rather than addressing the actual root cause
The vulnerability may live in the model weights or training data rather than application code, requiring rollback and lineage tracing to find other affected models
Because standard code-level patches automatically propagate to model weights, so lineage tracing is only needed to update documentation afterward
Because model checkpoints are rolled back purely to satisfy compliance logging requirements, not because the prior checkpoint is functionally safer

quiz.question: According to the pattern described, what typically causes teams to get caught flat-footed by a new adversarial technique?
options: Their original threat model relied on OWASP's categories instead of a stage-based framework like ATLAS, which OWASP's own documentation advises against
Their incident-response team lacked sufficient dedicated headcount to review the ATLAS catalog on any kind of recurring schedule
Their threat model was never revisited after it was first written, even as the ATLAS catalog and OWASP's risk list kept evolving with new documented techniques
They deployed a newer model version than the one their original MITRE ATLAS mapping and threat model had actually been validated against
